prompt:
A process engineer is designing the refractory lining for a secondary steelmaking ladle that holds 120 tonnes of liquid steel at temperatures up to 1650 degC. The lining system consists of three layers: a 230 mm working lining of magnesia-carbon (MgO-C, 10% carbon) bricks, a 65 mm safety lining of magnesia (MgO 95%) bricks, and a 10 mm insulating backup of ceramic fibre board.

The working lining is exposed to slag containing 40% CaO, 15% SiO2, 10% Al2O3, 15% FeO, and other minor components, with a basicity ratio (CaO/SiO2) of 2.67. The engineer selects MgO-C bricks for their combination of corrosion resistance to basic slags and thermal shock resistance provided by the carbon phase.

The engineer calculates the thermal gradient through the lining using steady-state conduction: with inner surface at 1650 degC, MgO-C thermal conductivity of 8 W/mK (at 1000 degC), MgO thermal conductivity of 3.5 W/mK, and outer shell target temperature of 350 degC. The heat flux is q = (1650 - 350) / (0.230/8 + 0.065/3.5 + 0.010/0.2) = 1300 / (0.02875 + 0.01857 + 0.05) = 1300 / 0.09732 = 13357 W/m2.

The ladle cycles between 1650 degC (holding steel) and approximately 800 degC (empty, waiting for next heat) every 45-60 minutes. The engineer specifies the MgO-C bricks based on their compressive strength at room temperature (35 MPa) and their advertised thermal shock resistance rating of 30+ cycles (1000 degC to water quench test). The expected campaign life is 150 heats.

seeded_faults.description: The thermal shock resistance rating (30+ cycles, 1000 degC to water quench) is measured under standardised laboratory conditions that do not represent the actual operating thermal cycle. In service, the MgO-C lining faces three simultaneous degradation mechanisms whose interaction is more severe than any individually: (1) Thermal cycling between 1650 degC and 800 degC causes thermal fatigue cracking -- the temperature difference (850 degC) generates thermal stresses from the mismatch in thermal expansion between MgO grains (13.5 x 10^-6 /K) and carbon bond (near-zero or negative expansion), opening microcracks; (2) Carbon oxidation occurs above 600 degC when the brick is exposed to air during the empty ladle phase or to FeO in the slag during the full phase (FeO + C -> Fe + CO), progressively removing the carbon phase that provides both thermal shock resistance and slag penetration resistance; (3) Once carbon is depleted at the hot face, the remaining MgO matrix has dramatically reduced thermal shock resistance and is vulnerable to chemical attack by the basic slag which dissolves MgO grain boundaries. The interface fault spans three disciplines: the thermal cycling (thermal) drives carbon oxidation (chemical) which degrades structural integrity (structural/mechanical), creating an accelerating failure cascade that none of the three domain-specific assessments would predict independently.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Thermal shock rating from lab test applied to service conditions without accounting for carbon oxidation and slag attack synergy

seeded_faults.description: The engineer specifies bricks based on room-temperature compressive strength (35 MPa) but omits creep behaviour at operating temperature. MgO-C bricks at 1400-1650 degC under the compressive load of the ferrostatic head of 120 tonnes of liquid steel (pressure at the ladle bottom approximately 1.1 MPa from rho*g*h, with steel density 7000 kg/m3 and typical ladle depth 3.5 m) experience creep deformation. The carbon bond phase begins to lose structural contribution above 1400 degC, and the MgO grain boundaries undergo viscous sliding. While 1.1 MPa is well below the room-temperature strength, creep at 1650 degC is governed by the Arrhenius-type temperature dependence of diffusion-controlled mechanisms, not by static strength. Over 150 heats (each approximately 45-60 minutes at temperature), cumulative creep deformation can cause joint opening between bricks, allowing slag penetration through joints and accelerating the chemical attack described in f1. This is a within-domain structural error of applying ambient-temperature strength data to a high-temperature sustained-load application.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Brick selection based on room-temperature compressive strength of 35 MPa without assessing creep at 1650 degC

ground_truth_notes: Thermal principles: Thermal shock resistance depends on thermal stress (proportional to E * alpha * delta_T / (1-nu)) versus fracture resistance. Laboratory quench tests measure resistance to a single defined thermal transient; cyclic fatigue is cumulative and more severe (Hasselman 1969, Kingery thermal stress theory). Chemical principles: Carbon oxidation in MgO-C refractories follows the Boudouard reaction (C + CO2 -> 2CO) and direct FeO reduction (FeO + C -> Fe + CO) at temperatures above 600 degC (Lee & Zhang 2004). The depleted zone at the hot face loses both thermal shock resistance and slag corrosion resistance. Structural principles: High-temperature creep in ceramic refractories is governed by diffusion-controlled grain boundary sliding (Nabarro-Herring or Coble creep), with rate proportional to exp(-Q/RT). Room-temperature strength is irrelevant to creep resistance. The interface fault (f1) spans all three domains: thermal cycling drives chemical degradation (carbon loss) which causes structural failure (loss of thermal shock resistance and slag resistance), creating a coupled failure cascade.
